query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high‐entropy alloys, when subjected to demanding service conditions (e.g., high strain rates or elevated temperatures), localized stress concentrations—especially at grain boundaries—trigger an accumulation of stacking faults that drive small-scale fcc‐to‐hcp transformations and promote nanosegregation of embrittling elements. These local changes, which do not occur under quasi‐static ambient conditions, compromise the normally robust intrinsic toughening mechanisms (such as dislocation slip and nano‐bridging), resulting in an abrupt loss of toughness and a shift toward brittle, intergranular fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase face‐centered cubic high‐entropy alloy (for example, CrMnFeCoNi) with a homogeneous microstructure and conventional ductile deformation mechanisms at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled mechanical loading regimes including high strain rates and elevated temperatures that mimic demanding engineering service conditions.
generation.conditions: Tests performed at room temperature and under quasi‐static loading serve as the baseline; compared with tests at, for instance, temperatures above 400°C and/or strain rates significantly higher than quasi‐static values, where local stress concentrations are expected to intensify.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of nanoscale hcp regions at stress concentrations and enhanced nanosegregation of embrittling solutes at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under high-demand conditions, the accumulation of stacking faults at localized stress concentrators (especially near GBs) lowers the energy barrier for a partial fcc-to-hcp transformation. Simultaneously, stress-driven solute redistribution leads to nanosegregation of elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, Mn) at grain boundaries, degrading intergranular cohesion. The combined effect curtails dislocation motion and crack-bridging mechanisms, thereby switching the failure mode from ductile to brittle.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline samples (room temperature, quasi‐static loading), samples tested under the demanding conditions will show: (1) a reduction in work hardening and toughness; (2) microstructural evidence (via TEM and APT) for localized hcp phase patches and measurable nanosegregation at GBs; and (3) fracture surfaces shifting from predominantly ductile transgranular features (e.g., dimpling and nano-bridging) to brittle intergranular cracking.
generation.baseline: The original single‐phase HEA under ambient conditions exhibits a synergy of dislocation slip, stacking fault formation, and crack‐bridging (e.g., nanotwinning) that imparts high toughness and ductility.
generation.boundary: The transition is expected once the applied stress/strain rate and/or temperature exceed a critical threshold – for example, temperatures >400°C or strain rates >>10^(-4) s^(-1) – where stress-induced stacking fault accumulation and grain boundary nanosegregation become pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from dual-phase TRIP studies (e.g., PMC7012927::web::018::discussion) and observations of GB-driven ductility loss in single-phase HEAs (PMC6897545::web::005::ductility_loss_accompanied_by_gb_crackin) support the role of stress-induced phase changes and segregation, it is uncertain whether the same mechanism quantitatively controls toughness loss in the intended single-phase systems. Extending the mechanism observed in dual-phase alloys to single-phase HEAs is the new aspect of this proposal.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical single-phase HEA specimens. Subject one set to quasi-static and room-temperature tensile testing (baseline) and the other set to elevated temperature and high strain-rate tensile testing. Immediately after testing, employ high-resolution TEM and atom probe tomography (APT) to map local phase composition and grain boundary chemistry. Correlate the mechanical test results (stress–strain curves and fracture surface features) with the microstructural analyses.
measurements: Stress–strain response (yield strength, work hardening rate, fracture strain, toughness)
TEM imaging of defect structures (stacking faults, nano-twins, hcp phase patches) around grain boundaries
APT analysis for detecting nanosegregation of elements at grain boundaries
Fractographic analysis (comparing ductile vs. intergranular fracture features)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens under demanding conditions display no significant difference in toughness compared to the baseline, and microstructural analysis fails to reveal any localized fcc-to-hcp transformation or enhanced grain boundary nanosegregation, then the hypothesis that these mechanisms drive the loss of toughness is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Using in situ atomic/nanoscale experimental observations, we have found that the exceptional damage tolerance of the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy can be principally associated with a novel synergistic sequence of plastic deformation mechanisms at different stages of strain that are the source of its excellent combination of strength, ductility and toughness. In general, toughness or fracture resistance can be considered to result from two classes of mechanisms: ‘intrinsic toughening' mechanisms, which are primarily associated with plasticity (and the generation of ductility) and operate ahead of the crack tip to provide resistance to microstructural damage, and ‘extrinsic toughening' mechanisms, which operate principally in the wake of the crack tip to inhibit fracture by ‘shielding' the crack from the applied driving force. Intrinsic toughening is most effective in ductile materials; it is inherent to the material and is effective in inhibiting both the initiation and growth of cracks. In summary, our results demonstrate that in the dual-phase Cantor-like high-entropy alloy, it is the continuous in situ phase transformation that provides the dominant contribution to strain hardening. As distinct from traditional dual-phase alloys, in the DP-HEAs the motivation for this transformation lies in the creation of stacking-fault networks, which seed the fcc → hcp transformation and which are intrinsically formed because of the fluctuation in lattice friction associated with concentration waves. However, it is worth noting that the fracture toughness of these TRIP HEAs may not be similarly enhanced compared to the Cantor alloy, particularly at decreasing temperatures. Despite the stress-induced TRIP effect of the fcc → hcp transformation, which acts to enhance the degree of strain hardening to the benefit of strength and ductility, fracture toughness is also a function of the inherent toughness of the product hcp phase, and this ε-martensite phase, despite its strength, tends to be quite brittle and not characterized by any significant degree of toughness.
